summary: Add multistep exam practice and more useful teaching prompts for predicting and deducing unfamiliar elements.

improvements.why: Current deduction practice is mainly single-step short answers and MCQs; none asks the learner to justify a candidate against several physical and chemical clues in a structured response.
improvements.what: Add structured Deduce/Justify items with two or three linked clues, for example period from shell count, group from ionisation-energy or electron evidence, then an oxide/chloride reaction to select the element. Award separate marks for each inference and for rejecting a plausible rival; allow uncertainty if clues do not uniquely identify one element. Do not repeat the existing aluminium precipitate or silicon chloride questions.

improvements.why: Prediction practice mostly repeats Group 2 and rarely makes the learner apply a known pattern to a different unfamiliar group member.
improvements.what: Add one exam-style Predict/Explain item about an unfamiliar Group 1 member using outer-electron arrangement, radius and reactivity trends, and one item that asks for a cautious prediction plus the evidence or limitation behind it. Use clear mark schemes that distinguish observation, inference and explanation.

improvements.why: Both cards give the reasoning directly but have no discover questions; learners need to practise choosing a trend or discriminating clue before seeing the conclusion.
improvements.what: Add a discover question to each card. For prediction, ask which property of known group members gives a defensible prediction and why. For deduction, present two candidates fitting an initial clue and ask which additional observation would separate them. Keep answers consistent with the existing note and misconceptions.

improvements.why: Many current hints use the same generic three sentences and do not guide the specific chemical reasoning in the stem.
improvements.what: Add item-specific hints and concise explanations to the new questions: first direct attention to the relevant clue or trend, then suggest the comparison, then name the first inference without revealing the final identity or property.
